bib.title: Can Generalist Foundation Models Outcompete Special-Purpose Tuning? Case Study in Medicine

read.skipped: References skimmed only. No appendices exist (21 pages, main text plus references).

question: Can a generalist model such as GPT-4, steered only by systematic prompt engineering, match or beat specialist fine-tuned models on medical challenge benchmarks?
hypothesis: Prompting innovation can unlock deeper specialist capabilities in GPT-4 without domain fine-tuning or expert-curated content.
contributions: Medprompt: dynamic kNN few-shot, GPT-4 self-generated CoT, choice-shuffle ensemble
State of the art on all nine MultiMedQA multiple-choice datasets, over 90% on MedQA
Eyes-off holdout methodology for prompt engineering
Generalisation to six non-medical MMLU subjects and two NCLEX datasets

method.summary: Medprompt preprocesses a training set by embedding each question and having GPT-4 write a CoT and answer, keeping only items whose answer matches the label. At test time it retrieves 5 nearest neighbours as few-shot CoT exemplars, runs 5 calls each with shuffled answer choices, and takes the majority vote. Nothing is trained.

limits: Benchmark contamination or memorisation cannot be ruled out; the earlier MELD black-box test found no evidence but gives no guarantee.
Multiple-choice exam performance does not show real-world clinical efficacy.
Adaptation to non-multiple-choice tasks is proposed but not tested.
Better prompting may make remaining hallucinations harder to detect; bias and equity not assessed.
Ablation order is subjective and components are not independent; Shapley values left to future work.
Temperature, GPT-4 version, and exact prompts beyond the CoT template are not given; no seeds or confidence intervals.
Fig 4 and Fig 6 give different per-component increments.
Dated: GPT-4 as of 2023; later reasoning models are not covered.
